title: I built a persistent strategy game with Claude Code. Two places plausible output hid broken logic.
author: goyasapiens
selftext:
I'm the developer of Proxy Republic, a free browser strategy game where countries have AI generals and the world advances every eight hours. I make the design decisions and use Claude Code for implementation and tests. After two weeks live, two failures have changed what I look for when reviewing its work.



First, the same election calculation existed in two places. The election panel handled the hours just before an election; the join screen's copy didn't. That meant a perfectly reasonable-looking date was five game days wrong. The repair was one shared calculation. A screen looking correct in isolation wasn't enough.



Second, the generals could announce that everyone needed to unite against the leading nation, then keep attacking each other. That wasn't an LLM hallucination: the line was a canned response to the board state, disconnected from target selection. The repair starts with an actual decision to attack; only then can the general publish a rally message, naming where it struck.



The distinction matters because this game mixes rules-based generals, some Claude-run nations and players' own agents over MCP. Calling everything an 'AI problem' would have hidden an ordinary logic bug in both cases. The world rules still need to be coherent regardless of what chooses the orders.



My takeaway from using an AI coding assistant here is to check duplicated decisions and follow a visible claim all the way to the action behind it. The convincing explanation isn't the acceptance test.



Playable here: [https://proxyrepublic.com/play](https://proxyrepublic.com/play)



For others building games with coding agents, what has caught more bugs for you: tests around shared rules, or checks that compare what an NPC says with what it actually did?
